title: NVLink bisection bandwidth investigation and topology-aware placement notes
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures a targeted set of experiments to quantify NVLink/PCIe bisection bandwidth limitations we observed on p4/8+ GPU boxes and to validate topology-aware placement heuristics for the serving runtime. The goal is pragmatic: find easy rules-of-thumb we can bake into the runtime scheduler and deployment docs so model latency doesn't regress badly when customers scale from 4->8->16 GPUs.

Background and motivation:
- Several customer incidents (see JIRA-RI-1423) where throughput drops >30% when moving from 4 to 8 GPUs for transformer inference with KV cache.
- Prior notes looked at NCCL microbursts and interconnect saturation, but we lacked focused bisection bandwidth experiments that use realistic traffic patterns (KV cache streaming + attention key/value exchange).
- Hypothesis: the effective bisection bandwidth of the node's NVLink/PCIe fabric is the limiting factor when pipeline/tensor parallel partitions are split across the wrong switch/bridge. Two practical mitigations: (1) topology-aware GPU placement (co-locate partitions inside NVLink islands) and (2) small changes to NCCL/comm config (fanout/ring vs. tree) to reduce simultaneous cross-bisection pressure.

Test matrix (high level):
1) Hardware tested: 8x A100 80GB (DGX-like), 8x H100 (cloud instance type), and a heterogeneous 4xA100 + 4xA40 node (edge case).
2) Software stack: CUDA 12.2, NCCL 2.18, nsys 23.x, our runtime built from commit sha abc123 (PR 789 has scheduler changes).
3) Workloads:
   - Synthetic allreduce and allgather microbenchmarks (nccl-tests: all_reduce_perf, all_gather_perf) across varying message sizes (1KB -> 64MB) to map bandwidth curve vs. message size.
   - Model-stepped trace replay: record network traffic during a 1-step KV cache refresh and replay with controlled offsets to simulate pipeline/tensor hybrid comm.
   - Full inference runs with model shards (tensor parallel 2/4, pipeline 2/2) to measure end-to-end step latency/percentiles.
4) Placement permutations: co-located (NVLink island contiguous GPUs) vs. striped (inter-island spread). Also single process per node vs. per-GPU processes to test NCCL topology selection differences.

Repro steps (quick):
- Run nccl-tests (built with CUDA) pinned to device ordering that reflects placement: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3,...
- Example command: ./build/all_reduce_perf -b 1 -e 67108864 -f 2 -g 8 -t 100
- Capture NVSwitch stats: nvidia-smi nvlink --query-gpu=linkUtilization --loop-ms=1000 (where supported) and run nsys profile around the test: 
  nsys profile -o nvlink_test --capture-range=cudaProfilerApi -- sample_command_here
- Record link-level counters with nvidia-smi dmon or NVML where available.

Key instrumentation notes:
- Use nsys to capture PCIe % time and cudaMemcpy/peer copies. NCCL provides event hooks (NCCL_TRACE) to time collectives; enable NCCL_DEBUG=INFO for timestamps.
- Collect kernel timelines to separate compute vs comm overlap. If comm stalls align with peaks in nccl kernel times, that's evidence of link contention.
- Use tcpdump on the control plane process to correlate NCCL topology negotiation with observed traffic patterns (helps verify ring vs tree selection).

Representative observations (summary of runs on 8xA100):
- Synthetic all_reduce_perf saturates per-island NVLink bandwidth for large messages (>8MB) when GPUs are co-located, achieving ~85% of theoretical.
- When the same workload is run with GPUs striped across islands (2GPUs per island alternated), observed aggregate bisection throughput drops ~40% and 99th pct latency for the collective increases ~3-4x.
- Model-trace replay with many small KV messages (~4-64KB) shows a different regime: peak utilization is lower, but tail latency increases due to many concurrent small transfers crossing the bisection at the same time (microburst behavior).
- NCCL algorithm choice matters: by forcing ring (NCCL_ALGO=Ring) we saw slightly higher latency for small messages but more predictable throughput; tree algorithms gave better bandwidth for large messages but amplified microburst-induced tails for small messages.
- On the heterogeneous node (A100 + A40) the NIC-peer bandwidth asymmetry triggered NCCL to create suboptimal rings causing extra hops; topology-aware placement forcing same-class GPUs together eliminated this anomaly and restored expected scaling.

Concrete explanations / root causes:
- The effective bisection (i.e., total cross-island bandwidth available simultaneously) is much lower than the sum of per-link peak specs because of shared switches and PCIe bridge contention. Placing tensor-parallel partners across this bisection forces large all-reduce/all-gather payloads to compete on shared links.
- Small-message microbursts create queueing on the link buffers; tree algorithms that fan-in/fan-out amplify the instantaneous pressure because many leaves send concurrently into the bridge.

Actionable mitigations (short-term):
1) Topology-aware placement in runtime scheduler: prefer contiguous NVLink islands when assigning tensor parallel groups. Simple rule: when TP > 1, choose GPUs with minimal island crossings.
2) Default NCCL settings per message size: for small-message-heavy workloads (KV lookup dominated), prefer ring-based collectives or lower NCCL_IB_GDR_LEVEL to reduce cross-host funneling. Add per-model config toggle in runtime.
3) Add an admission control check during allocation that runs a quick nccl-test microbenchmark (1-2s) to detect pathological fabric layouts and recommend a different placement.
4) Document best-practices in deploy guide: GPU ordering (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES), affinity hints, and recommended instance families.

Longer-term work / experiments to run next:
- Evaluate use of NCCL P2P vs SHARP (on systems that support it) for large-model gradients/activations to see if switch-level aggregation reduces bisection pressure.
- Test congestion control knobs (NCCL_IB_TIMEOUT, NCCL_TUNING) impact on microburst tails.
- Integrate a lightweight topology discovery probe into onboarding so Dedicated/Private deployments publish a topology map we can use to optimize default placements automatically.

Open questions / things to verify:
- Does topology-aware placement always improve latency for mixed-size workloads or are there pathological workloads where spreading reduces contention on local caches and helps? Need synthetic + real traces.
- Quantify overhead of running an admission nccl-test on cold start and whether customers will accept the slight delay.

Immediate TODOs (owners):
- Miguel: add placement heuristic prototype into scheduler (PR stubbed at PR-789) - due 2025-11-24.
- Lina: run extended microburst sweep across message sizes (1KB-1MB) and capture nsys traces for 3 node types - due 2025-11-21.
- Ethan: add a simple admission-check CLI that runs a 2s all_reduce_perf and returns pass/fail - due 2025-11-20.

Notes to self / rough ideas (scratch):
- Could try a hybrid approach: map pipeline stages to NVLink islands and use tensor-parallel rings inside islands, then use a tree across islands but stagger schedule to avoid simultaneous fans.
- Consider exposing a "placement safety score" in the Console that warns customers when their requested node may cross bisection limits.

References and artifacts:
- nccl-tests repo: https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests (used for perf)
- Related internal ticket: JIRA-RI-1423
- PR with scheduler prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/789

Appendix: commands used (examples)
- build and run nccl perf: git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests.git && make -j && ./build/all_reduce_perf -b 1 -e 67108864 -f 2 -g 8 -t 50
- nsys capture around a python replay script: nsys profile -o nvlink_replay --trace=cuda python replay_kv_trace.py --devices 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7
- enable NCCL traces: export NCCL_DEBUG=INFO; export NCCL_ALGO=Automatic (or Ring/Tree)

End.
